title: What You Are Actually Measuring When You Benchmark Speculative Decoding Under FP8: A measurement case study on vLLM 0.29.0 and NVIDIA L4
description:
An independent measurement study of speculative decoding and FP8 quantization on vLLM 0.29.0 / NVIDIA L4 (SM89), released with the harness, the raw records, and the full history of its own corrections.

We set out to measure how FP8 quantization interacts with speculative decoding and could not, four times, until the measurement apparatus itself was fixed. Four confounds are identified and quantified:

  1. Attention-backend selection is conditioned on KV-cache dtype. At BF16 KV vLLM selects FlashAttention-2; at fp8_e4m3 it selects FlashInfer, so a precision A/B under default settings is also a kernel A/B. Target and draft models select independently, so pinning one does not pin the other.
  2. An identical speculative configuration lands in one of two session-scoped throughput regimes, and nothing we record predicts which. Across nine container sessions on nine distinct physical L4 cards, the ratio of CUDA-graph to --enforce-eager throughput measured in the same container splits into two disjoint groups: three sessions at 0.487–0.768 and six at 1.003–1.039, with nothing between. The same partition separates boot-to-boot dispersion of the graph arm (3.73–10.38% against 0.86–1.95%), so the deficit and the dispersion are one session-scoped phenomenon rather than two findings; the probability that the three highest-dispersion sessions are exactly the three lowest-ratio ones is 1/84 = 0.012. The separation also holds boot by boot: pooled over 116 individual boots the two groups do not overlap at all, with a 9.9 tok/s gap against a largest within-group gap of 5.7. Earlier releases read this split as a regression fixed between engine releases and this release withdraws that: three further 0.29.0 sessions reached parity, giving 3 deficit of 6 on 0.29.0 against 0 of 3 on later releases, one-sided Fisher p = 0.238. Engine release and measurement date are also entangled in our design, which we state rather than resolve.
  3. Acceptance length has a boot-to-boot coefficient of variation below 0.88% in every session we have run — nine sessions, three engine releases, both throughput regimes, mean tau within 2.2% throughout — which we could not find reported. That contrast is the point: on the same boots, what the drafter gets accepted is reproducible and how fast it is produced is not. The contrast is itself regime-dependent, which sharpens it: in deficit sessions throughput dispersion exceeds acceptance dispersion by 12–22x, while in parity sessions both are below 2%.
  4. "Inter-token latency" is inter-chunk latency when computed from stream-arrival timestamps. A speculative step emits every accepted token in one chunk, so at concurrency 64 a p95-ITL objective scores the highest-throughput configuration at zero compliant goodput, at every threshold from 20 to 75 ms. This one does not add error, it inverts the decision.

The first three add error; the fourth reverses the ranking.

On the mechanism. It remains unidentified, but the checkable candidates are eliminated by direct measurement rather than left unexamined. CUDA-graph mode and attention-backend selection are unchanged across the engine releases. Power throttling is refuted twice over by sampling the driver's own throttle reasons: across the two arms of a deficit session, where both arms are capped for 84–95% of samples and the faster arm is capped more at a lower clock drawing more power; and across regimes on the same arm, where deficit graph arms hold a clock 177–291 MHz higher than any parity graph arm while producing 23–31% fewer tokens, drawing less power and being capped less often. A card that boosts higher and delivers less work is not against a ceiling. The stall reading this implies remains untested: GPU-utilisation sampling was added after the last deficit session occurred, so we have the prediction and the parity baseline (90.5–91.6%) and not the measurement.

Contents of this archive: the LaTeX source and PDF of the paper; 40 numbered findings, of which 8 are formal retractions and several more withdraw a reading of their own predecessor, each carrying a mandatory "what this does NOT establish" section; the raw append-only measurement records; the analysis scripts that derive every table in the paper from those records; and the audit scripts that verify every numeric claim traces to a stored record and that no finding rests on terminal output.

Reproducibility: every result is re-derivable by a third party on rented hardware. Requires a CUDA GPU of compute capability 8.6 or above and roughly 22 GiB of VRAM. The harness never imports the engine; it launches vLLM as a separate server process and speaks only HTTP. Engine version, physical GPU identity, and achieved clocks, power draw and utilisation during the measurement window are recorded per measurement. Two disclosed provenance defects (F009, F014) rest on probe output predating per-measurement recording; neither is cited in the paper and both are disclosed in its threats section.

Licensing: the harness and analysis code are MIT (see LICENSE). The measurements, findings and the paper are CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSE-DATA). The split is deliberate: the harness should be reusable with minimal friction, and the scientific record should carry attribution.

This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed.
notes: Measurements were taken on rented NVIDIA L4 and A10 instances. Physical GPU identity (gpu_uuid) has been recorded per measurement since 2026-09-29, achieved SM clock, power draw and driver throttle reasons across the measurement window since 2026-10-04, and GPU utilisation since 2026-10-31; measurements taken before those dates lack the corresponding fields, and the paper states which of its claims are replicated and which are single-session draws. Every session reported here ran on a distinct physical card, so no regime can be attributed to a specific card. Zenodo's GitHub integration adds its own isSupplementTo relation to the release, so this file deliberately declares none.
